objectives: Distinguish substance + properties + universals (Plato realism, Aristotle moderate realism, nominalism).
Understand modality + possible worlds — Kripke 1972, Lewis 1986 modal realism, necessary a posteriori.
Reason about time + persistence (endurantism vs perdurantism, presentism vs eternalism) + free will (Frankfurt, Pereboom).

slides.title: Substance, properties, universals — Plato, Aristotle, nominalism
slides.body:
**Metaphysics** = the systematic inquiry into the fundamental categories of reality. What is there? What are its kinds + structures? What is real, and what is mere appearance?

**Substance + property — the first divide**. From Aristotle's ***Categories*** + ***Metaphysics*** onward: a **substance** is a thing that exists in itself (Socrates, this oak, this water molecule); a **property** is what is *predicated of* a substance ('Socrates is wise', 'the oak is tall', 'the water is cold'). Substance is *primary*; properties are *dependent*. Properties can be **monadic** (the oak is tall) or **relational** (Socrates is taller than Plato).

**The problem of universals — three positions**. *What grounds the fact that many particulars share a property?* Many things are *red*, many are *triangular*, many are *human*. What is *redness*? *triangularity*? *humanity*?

**1. Platonic realism (extreme / ante rem realism)**: Plato (*Republic*, *Phaedo*, *Parmenides*). **Forms** are eternal, unchanging, mind-independent, abstract entities. Particulars are red, triangular, human by *participating* in the Forms of Red, Triangle, Human. Forms exist *prior to + apart from* their instances. Mathematical Platonism (Frege, Gödel, Quine in certain moods) is a descendant — numbers, sets, functions are abstract entities. Powerful but raises hard questions: how do spatiotemporal particulars relate to non-spatiotemporal abstracts? How do we know about them?

**2. Aristotelian moderate realism (in re realism)**: Aristotle, ***Metaphysics*** Books Z + H. Forms (or universals) exist *only in* their particulars; you cannot have *redness* without *some red thing*. Universals are immanent — *in* substances, not in a separate realm. *Hylomorphism*: a substance is form + matter (the form of the bronze statue + the bronze). Avoids Platonic 'two-world' problem; saves universals as genuine constituents of reality. Dominant medieval position (Aquinas) + lives on in contemporary metaphysics (Armstrong's *Universals + Scientific Realism* 1978).

**3. Nominalism**: only particulars exist; *redness* is just a *name* (Latin *nomen*) for a class of red things. Several variants:
- **Predicate nominalism**: 'is red' applies to many things; no further entity needed.
- **Class nominalism**: the universal *redness* is just the class of red things (problems: coextensive properties collapse).
- **Resemblance nominalism** (Rodriguez-Pereyra 2002): red things resemble certain paradigm cases.
- **Trope theory** (D. C. Williams 1953, Campbell 1990, Maurin): *this particular redness instance* (the redness *of this particular tomato*) is the basic entity; substances are bundles of compresent tropes. Properties are abstract particulars.
- **Conceptualism / mental nominalism** (Locke, Berkeley): universals are mental concepts only.

**W. V. O. Quine** — **'On What There Is' (1948)**: ontology is just what your best scientific theory quantifies over. 'To be is to be the value of a bound variable.' Quine was a nominalist-leaning naturalist; co-authored *Set-Theoretic Foundations for a Logic of Higher-Order Properties* (1986) hesitantly admitting sets. Quine reshaped the analytic ontological debate by tying it to logical form + scientific practice.

**Bundle vs substratum theory of objects**: is a particular *just* a bundle of properties (bundle theory — Hume, Russell at points, Castañeda) or are properties *had by* an underlying bare particular / substratum (Locke, Bergmann, Sider)? Each faces classical objections — bundle theory: identity of indiscernibles + necessary co-instantiation; substratum theory: what is a *bare* particular like?

**Composition + mereology**: when do parts compose a whole? Trenton Merricks (*Objects + Persons* 2001) — eliminativism about ordinary objects. Peter van Inwagen (*Material Beings* 1990) — composition only when the parts constitute a life. Theodore Sider — unrestricted composition (Lewis-style four-dimensionalism). The **special composition question**. **Ship of Theseus** + sorites paradoxes for ordinary objects.

**Modern systematic metaphysics — Quine, Lewis, Armstrong, Kim, van Inwagen, Sider, Schaffer** has reanimated all these debates with logical + scientific rigor. *Metaphysics* is no longer a derelict subject (as logical positivism declared in the 1930s); it is one of the most active areas of analytic philosophy.

slides.title: Modality + possible worlds — Kripke, Lewis (David), necessary a posteriori
slides.body:
**Modality** = necessity ($\Box$) + possibility ($\Diamond$). *Necessarily $p$*: $p$ is true in every possible state of affairs. *Possibly $p$*: $p$ is true in some possible state of affairs. The interplay of *necessary*, *possible*, *contingent*, + *impossible* shapes metaphysics, epistemology + philosophy of language.

**Classical positions**:
- **De dicto modality**: 'necessarily, all bachelors are unmarried' (the necessity attaches to the proposition).
- **De re modality**: of Aristotle, necessarily he is human (the necessity attaches to the thing). Quine famously skeptical of *de re* modality; Kripke + Lewis rehabilitated it.
- **Logical** (true in virtue of logical form), **conceptual / analytic** (true in virtue of meaning), **mathematical**, **metaphysical**, **physical / nomological** (true given the actual laws of nature), **epistemic** ('for all I know'), **historical** modalities. Distinct + sometimes conflated.

**Possible worlds semantics — Kripke 1959 + 1963**. Saul Kripke gave a model-theoretic semantics for modal logic: a frame $(W, R)$ with worlds $W$ + an accessibility relation $R$. $\Box \phi$ is true at $w$ iff $\phi$ is true at every $w'$ with $w R w'$. Different axiom systems (K, T, S4, S5) correspond to different properties of $R$ (reflexivity, transitivity, symmetry). The most cited contribution of any 19-year-old in the history of logic. Foundational for modal logic, dynamic + temporal + epistemic logics, formal verification, distributed-systems semantics.

**Kripke, *Naming and Necessity* (1972/1980)** extended modal logic into metaphysics + philosophy of language (lesson 2).
- **Rigid designation**: proper names designate the same object in every possible world in which the object exists.
- **Necessary a posteriori**: 'water = H₂O', 'Hesperus = Phosphorus', 'gold has atomic number 79', 'this lectern was made of wood' — *necessary* (true in every possible world) but known *a posteriori* (through empirical investigation). Repudiates the Kantian assumption that necessary truths are knowable a priori.
- **Contingent a priori**: 'the standard meter is one meter long' (under a specific stipulation about how the meter is fixed). Knowable a priori (by stipulation) but contingent (could have been otherwise).
- **Origin essentialism**: this table is necessarily made from the wood it was actually made from.
- **Natural-kind essentialism**: water is necessarily H₂O; tigers are necessarily of a particular biological kind.

**David Lewis (1941-2001) + modal realism — ***On the Plurality of Worlds*** (1986)**: the most ambitious + provocative metaphysical book of the late 20th century. Lewis: possible worlds are *concrete, real, spatiotemporally + causally isolated universes* — not abstract objects, not 'ways the world could be', but full-blown alternate cosmoses. Modal truths reduce to truths about which worlds exist + what they are like. Why accept it? **Theoretical utility** — modal logic, propositions as sets of worlds, properties as sets of possibilia, counterfactuals, causation all reduce to first-order facts about pluralities of worlds. Lewis's *quantifier* analysis: 'possibly $\phi$' = there is a world at which $\phi$. Includes counterpart theory (no individual exists at multiple worlds; each world has counterparts of actual individuals).

**Critics + alternatives**:
- **Ersatz / actualist possibilism** (Plantinga, Adams, Stalnaker, Sider): worlds are abstract — maximal consistent sets of propositions, or maximal states of affairs, or maximal properties the universe could instantiate. All worlds 'exist' in the way numbers exist, not as concrete cosmoses.
- **Combinatorialism** (Armstrong *A Combinatorial Theory of Possibility* 1989): worlds are recombinations of actual elements.
- **Modalism** (Forbes, Peacocke): modal facts are basic; possible-worlds talk is just a convenient device.
- **Fictionalism** (Rosen 1990): possible worlds are useful fiction, not real.

**Modal epistemology — how do we know modal truths?** Conceivability + possibility (Chalmers 2002 *Does Conceivability Entail Possibility?*); intuition (Bealer); essentialism + necessary a posteriori (Kripke). Linked to zombie + Mary's-Room arguments in philosophy of mind (lesson 6).

**Modality in physics + science**: laws of nature as physical necessities; the multiverse interpretations of QM + cosmology; computational + algorithmic modality (what's computable / possible to compute). Modality is the bridge between metaphysics + physics + epistemology + language.

slides.title: Time, persistence, free will — endurantism vs perdurantism, presentism vs eternalism, Frankfurt + Pereboom
slides.body:
**Persistence**: how does a thing persist through time? Two main views:

**Endurantism (3-dimensionalism)**: an object exists *wholly* at each time at which it exists. There is one whole Socrates that exists at $t_1$ + the same whole Socrates that exists at $t_2$. Changes are had by the persistent entity; properties are time-indexed (Socrates-at-$t_1$ is young; Socrates-at-$t_2$ is old). Aligns with common sense + Aristotelian substance metaphysics.

**Perdurantism (4-dimensionalism)** — David Lewis (*On the Plurality of Worlds* 1986), Theodore Sider (*Four-Dimensionalism* 2001): an object persists by having distinct **temporal parts** at distinct times. Socrates is a 4-dimensional 'space-time worm'; Socrates-at-$t_1$ + Socrates-at-$t_2$ are different parts of one extended whole. Naturally accommodates special relativity, modal logic, change-without-contradiction, the puzzle of fission (split-brain, branching-self cases). The dominant view among analytic metaphysicians.

**Stage theory** (Sider, Hawley): only momentary stages exist; persistence is a matter of counterpart-relations between stages.

**Theories of time itself**:

**Presentism**: only the present is real; past + future are not. Defenders: Prior, Bigelow, Bourne, Markosian, Crisp. Aligns with common sense + the felt 'now'. Tensions with special relativity (no privileged simultaneity).

**Eternalism (block universe)**: past, present, + future are all equally real; 'now' is indexical, like 'here'. Aligns naturally with Einsteinian space-time. Most contemporary physicists + many analytic metaphysicians. Quine, Lewis, Sider.

**Growing-block theory** (Broad, Tooley): past + present are real; the future is not, but new slices accrue. Compromise position.

**Moving spotlight**: eternalism + a moving objective 'now' (Cameron). Conserves both physics + the felt now.

**Tense + the A-series vs B-series** — McTaggart, *The Unreality of Time* (1908): the **A-series** ranks events as past / present / future (tensed); the **B-series** ranks them as earlier-than / later-than (tenseless). McTaggart argued the A-series is contradictory + so time is unreal. Modern responses: B-theorists embrace tenseless time; A-theorists give detensed reformulations. Still debated.

**Time travel + closed causal loops**: Lewis 'The Paradoxes of Time Travel' (1976); Gödel's rotating universes with closed timelike curves; grandfather paradox + branching solutions. Mostly metaphysical, occasionally physical (GR + quantum gravity).

**Free will** — perhaps the most consequential metaphysical question + the one with the largest popular + ethical + legal stakes.

**Determinism**: every event is fully determined by prior events + the laws of nature. Quantum mechanics complicates the picture (genuinely indeterministic on standard interpretations); but **adequate determinism** at the relevant scales for human behavior holds on most views.

**Compatibilism**: free will is *compatible* with determinism. Free actions are those that flow from the agent's *own* will + practical reasoning, unimpeded by coercion + compulsion. Defenders: Hobbes, Hume, Mill, Ayer, **Harry Frankfurt** (lesson reference!), Daniel Dennett (*Elbow Room* 1984; *Freedom Evolves* 2003), Susan Wolf (*Freedom Within Reason* 1990), John Martin Fischer + Mark Ravizza (*Responsibility and Control* 1998 — reasons-responsiveness).

**Harry Frankfurt's 'Alternate Possibilities and Moral Responsibility' (1969)** — the **Frankfurt cases**: an agent has a backup mechanism that would force her to do $A$ if she didn't choose $A$ on her own; but in fact she chooses $A$ on her own. She had no alternative possibility (couldn't have done otherwise), yet she is morally responsible. Therefore moral responsibility does *not* require alternative possibilities — challenging the **Principle of Alternate Possibilities (PAP)**. Hugely influential.

**Frankfurt 'Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person' (1971)** — **hierarchical theory of free will**: a free agent has **second-order volitions** (desires about which first-order desires to be effective). Addiction case (the willing vs unwilling addict). Influential in ethics + philosophy of mind + AI agent design.

**Libertarianism** (about free will, not politics): free will exists + is incompatible with determinism. Robert Kane (*The Significance of Free Will* 1996) — agent causation + self-forming actions; Roderick Chisholm; Timothy O'Connor. Requires either substance causation (the *agent* as an irreducible cause) or quantum indeterminism amplified at the neural level.

**Hard determinism + hard incompatibilism — Derk Pereboom (*Living Without Free Will* 2001; *Free Will, Agency, and Meaning in Life* 2014)**: even if determinism were false, *no* account of free will gives us what we need for moral responsibility in the strong (basic-desert) sense. Manipulation arguments — if a master manipulator can shape your every action through perfectly causal means, you're not responsible; but causal determinism is just a more diffuse manipulator. Hence we should abandon basic-desert moral responsibility — but can keep forward-looking notions (deterrence, rehabilitation, character formation). Galen Strawson (*Freedom and Belief* 1986) — the *basic argument* — gives a similar conclusion. Has serious consequences for the criminal-justice system + everyday moral practice.

**Modern empirical work**: Benjamin Libet (1980s) — brain activity preceding 'conscious decisions'; replicated + debated. Daniel Wegner *The Illusion of Conscious Will* (2002). Neuroscience + psychology constrain but do not settle the metaphysical question. The modern frontier of free-will philosophy integrates analytic metaphysics, cognitive science, ethics, law, AI agent design + alignment (lesson 8).

question.question: Argue through Kripke's necessary a posteriori claim about water = H₂O
question.goal: Show how Kripke's modal + semantic + scientific apparatus delivers necessary a posteriori identities.

acceptedAnswers: we learned that water is h2o through 18th-century chemistry (cavendish, lavoisier); no amount of reflection on the concept of water yields the molecular formula

steps.reveal: We did not know that water = H₂O until 18th-century chemistry (Cavendish 1781 — hydrogen as 'inflammable air'; Lavoisier 1783 — water as compound; Dalton + Avogadro fixing atomic + molecular counts in the early 19th c.). The identity is established by empirical chemistry, not by reflection on the concept *water*. So it's *a posteriori*.

steps.prompt: Why does Kripke nonetheless say it's necessary?

acceptedAnswers: 'water' and 'h2o' are both rigid designators referring to the same natural kind in every possible world; if a = b and a, b are rigid, then necessarily a = b

hints: If identity holds + designators are rigid, identity holds in every world.
steps.reveal:
Kripke 1972: proper names + natural-kind terms are **rigid designators** — they designate the same object / kind in every possible world. 'Water' refers to the actual substance H₂O (fixed by causal-historical baptism + chemical investigation). 'H₂O' refers to the same chemical compound. If a = b and both 'a' + 'b' are rigid, then in every world in which a + b exist, a = b. So 'water = H₂O' is true in every possible world — it is **necessary**.

There's no possible world where the watery stuff is XYZ + *still water* — by Putnam-Kripke semantics, that world contains a different natural kind that resembles water, not water itself.

steps.prompt: What does this show about the Kantian a priori / necessary alignment?

acceptedAnswers: kant held necessary truths are a priori and contingent are a posteriori; kripke severs the link — there are necessary a posteriori (water = h2o, hesperus = phosphorus, origin essentialism) and contingent a priori (the standard meter)

hints: Kant's apparent identification of necessary with a priori.
steps.reveal: Kant (*Critique of Pure Reason* 1781) had largely identified the necessary with the a priori + the contingent with the a posteriori. Kripke severs this: there are **necessary a posteriori** truths ('water = H₂O', 'Hesperus = Phosphorus', 'this lectern is wood', 'gold has atomic number 79') + **contingent a priori** truths ('the standard meter is one meter long' under the meter-bar stipulation). This restructures the modal-epistemic landscape + revives essentialism — natural kinds have *essences* discovered empirically + holding necessarily.

steps.motivation: Natural kinds + modal realism + Putnam externalism.

acceptedAnswers: natural-kind essentialism (gold, water, tigers); origin essentialism (this table from this wood); arguments in philosophy of mind (zombie + property dualism); foundation of lewis modal realism vs ersatz alternatives

steps.reveal: Consequences: (1) natural-kind essentialism (water, gold, tigers, electrons necessarily have their actual essences); (2) origin essentialism (Aristotle's parents are essentially his parents; this table is essentially from this wood); (3) the apparatus of necessary a posteriori is used in the **zombie argument** + **Mary's Room** in philosophy of mind (Chalmers, Jackson — lesson 6) to argue against physicalism: if zombies are *conceivable* + conceivability tracks possibility, physicalism is false; (4) modal realism vs ersatz possibilism (Lewis 1986 vs Plantinga, Stalnaker, Adams) becomes the main debate about possible-worlds ontology; (5) Putnam content externalism (lesson 2) shares the underlying rigid-designator + causal-theory architecture.

question.question: Why is David Lewis's *On the Plurality of Worlds* (1986) considered the most ambitious work of late-20th-century metaphysics?
options: **David Lewis (1941-2001), ***On the Plurality of Worlds*** (1986)** argued for **modal realism** — possible worlds are *concrete, real, spatiotemporally + causally isolated universes*, not abstract objects, not 'ways the world could be'. Every way our world could have been is a way some other world *actually* is. Why accept such an outrageous-seeming view? **Theoretical utility**: modal claims reduce to first-order quantifications over worlds + their inhabitants. Propositions = sets of worlds; properties = sets of possibilia; counterfactuals = closest-world truth conditions (Lewis 1973 *Counterfactuals*); causation = counterfactual dependence; laws = best-system summaries (Humean supervenience); essence + de re modality via counterpart theory. The reduction is breathtaking + works on a wider range of cases than ersatz alternatives (Plantinga, Stalnaker, Adams, Sider — worlds as abstract maximal-consistent sets, maximal states of affairs, or maximal universe-properties). The book is famously the *defense* of Lewis's career-long systematic metaphysics — Humean supervenience, counterfactual analysis, conventionalism about laws + chance. Even philosophers who reject modal realism use Lewis's machinery; he reshaped what serious analytic metaphysics looks like + restored its centrality after positivism's mid-century dismissal.
question.explanation: Lewis's *On the Plurality of Worlds* (1986) argued for modal realism — possible worlds are concrete, real, spatiotemporally / causally isolated universes. Theoretical payoff: modal logic, propositions, properties, counterfactuals, causation, essence all reduce to first-order quantification over worlds. Even philosophers who reject the ontology use Lewis's machinery; the book restored analytic metaphysics's centrality.

hints: Modal realism — worlds as concrete cosmoses.
What does the ontology buy you theoretically?
slides.workedSolution: Lewis's *On the Plurality of Worlds* (1986) defended modal realism — possible worlds as concrete, real, spatiotemporally + causally isolated universes. Reduces modality, propositions, properties, counterfactuals (Lewis 1973), causation + laws to quantification over worlds. Ersatz alternatives (Plantinga, Stalnaker, Adams, Sider) treat worlds as abstract. Even critics use Lewis's machinery; the book restored systematic analytic metaphysics.

question.question: Free will + criminal justice
question.prompt: A state legislature is debating reforming sentencing in light of recent neuroscience + philosophy. Draft a ≤220-word policy brief that draws on (a) compatibilism — Frankfurt 1969 cases (no alternate-possibilities requirement) + 1971 hierarchical free will + reasons-responsiveness (Fischer + Ravizza 1998); (b) hard incompatibilism — Pereboom *Living Without Free Will* (2001) — manipulation arguments + abandonment of basic-desert moral responsibility; (c) libertarianism — Kane *The Significance of Free Will* (1996); + (d) the empirical work (Libet, Wegner). Recommend two specific policy directions (e.g., emphasize rehabilitation + forward-looking deterrence over retributive punishment; preserve responsibility frameworks for practical reasons; cautious about neuroscience over-claims) + name one philosophical question that remains genuinely open.

question.question: Modal logic axiom systems are built from $\Box$ (necessarily) + $\Diamond$ (possibly), with $\Diamond \phi \equiv \neg \Box \neg \phi$. In S5, the axiom $\Diamond \phi \to \Box \Diamond \phi$ holds — if possibly $\phi$, then necessarily possibly $\phi$. If the accessibility relation in S5 is an **equivalence relation** (reflexive, symmetric, transitive), how many distinct modalities can be expressed by iterating $\Box$ + $\Diamond$? (E.g. $\Box \Box \phi$ collapses to $\Box \phi$.)
question.hint:
In S5 every modal iteration collapses to one of: $\phi$, $\Box \phi$, $\Diamond \phi$, $
eg \phi$, $\Box 
eg \phi$, $\Diamond 
eg \phi$ — i.e. **6 distinct modalities** (or 3 if we ignore negation). S5 = full reduction of iterated modalities. Kripke (1959, 1963) gave the model-theoretic semantics + the correspondence between axiom systems + frame properties. S5 = equivalence-relation accessibility; S4 = reflexive + transitive (preorder); KT = reflexive; etc. Foundation of philosophical + linguistic + computational uses of modality (lesson 2).

question.prompt: In ≤140 words, characterize analytic metaphysics by naming (a) the universals problem + the three positions (Plato realism, Aristotle moderate realism, nominalism — Quine, trope theory); (b) Kripke 1972 *Naming and Necessity* + David Lewis 1986 *On the Plurality of Worlds* + necessary a posteriori; (c) endurantism vs perdurantism + presentism vs eternalism + Frankfurt 1969-71 + Pereboom 2001 on free will.
question.rubric: Mentions: universals — Plato realism (*Republic*, *Phaedo*); Aristotle moderate / in-re realism (*Metaphysics* Z + H); nominalism — Quine 'On What There Is' (1948), trope theory (D. C. Williams 1953, Campbell 1990), Armstrong *Universals + Scientific Realism* (1978). Modality — Kripke 1959 + 1963 possible-worlds semantics + *Naming and Necessity* (1972) rigid designators + necessary a posteriori + contingent a priori + natural-kind essentialism; Lewis *On the Plurality of Worlds* (1986) modal realism vs ersatz alternatives (Plantinga, Stalnaker, Adams). Time + persistence — endurantism vs perdurantism (Lewis 1986, Sider 2001 *Four-Dimensionalism*); presentism vs eternalism + growing block; McTaggart A-series / B-series. Free will — Frankfurt 1969 (Frankfurt cases + denial of PAP) + 1971 (hierarchical theory); Pereboom 2001 *Living Without Free Will* hard incompatibilism + manipulation arguments; Kane 1996 libertarianism; Fischer + Ravizza 1998 reasons-responsiveness; Libet 1980s empirical work. Concludes that analytic metaphysics integrates ontology + modality + time + agency into a single rigorous enterprise.
